entity_designations.entity: Hoshine Silicon Industry (Shanshan) Co., Ltd (alias: Hesheng Silicon Industry (Shanshan) Co.) and subsidiaries
entity_designations.basis: Listed under Section 2(d)(2)(B)(i) (entities in Xinjiang that mine, produce or manufacture goods with forced labor) and also on the 2(d)(2)(B)(v) list (sourcing via 'poverty alleviation' / 'pairing-assistance' or other government labor schemes).

entity_designations.entity: Hoshine Silicon Industry Co. Ltd. and subsidiaries
entity_designations.basis: CBP found information 'reasonably indicating that Hoshine uses forced labor'; identified two ILO indicators: 'intimidation and threats, and restriction of movement'. Covers silica-based products and goods 'such as polysilicon' derived from them.

entity_designations.entity: Xinjiang Daqo New Energy, Co. Ltd (aliases: Xinjiang Great New Energy; Xinjiang Daxin Energy; Xinjiang Daqin Energy)
entity_designations.basis: Listed under Section 2(d)(2)(B)(i): entity in Xinjiang that mines, produces or manufactures goods wholly or in part with forced labor.

entity_designations.entity: Xinjiang East Hope Nonferrous Metals Co., Ltd.
entity_designations.basis: Listed under Section 2(d)(2)(B)(i). On 2024-11-25 a technical correction removed the alias 'Xinjiang Nonferrous', which is why DHS now shows an effective date of November 25, 2024.

entity_designations.entity: Xinjiang Goens Energy Technology Co., Ltd. (formerly Xinjiang GCL New Energy Material Technology Co., Ltd.)
entity_designations.basis: Originally listed under Section 2(d)(2)(B)(i) on June 21, 2022 as Xinjiang GCL; renamed via technical correction effective 2026-08-03 after the company 'changed its name'. Described as engaged in 'production, and sales of polysilicon and monocrystalline silicon'.

entity_designations.entity: Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps (XPCC; Xinjiang Corps; Bingtuan) and its subordinate and affiliated entities
entity_designations.basis: Listed under Section 2(d)(2)(B)(i) and named in the 2(d)(2)(B)(v) list heading for government labor schemes.

entity_designations.entity: Hoshine, Xinjiang Daqo, Xinjiang East Hope, Xinjiang GCL, and XPCC
entity_designations.basis: Added 'for accepting or utilizing forced labor' in the campaign of repression against Muslim minority groups in the XUAR; restricts their access to items subject to the EAR.

entity_designations.entity: TBEA Co., Ltd. (parent of polysilicon maker Xinte)
entity_designations.basis: Added under Section 2(d)(2)(B)(v): reasonable cause to believe TBEA 'sources aluminum and aluminum alloy products from the XUAR'. FR notes TBEA produces 'high-purity polysilicon'.

entity_designations.entity: Xinjiang Tianchi Energy Co., Ltd. (TBEA subsidiary)
entity_designations.basis: Added under Section 2(d)(2)(B)(v): reasonable cause to believe it 'sources coal from the XUAR'.

facts.statement: In 2020 polysilicon makers in the Uyghur Region produced about 45% of the world's solar-grade polysilicon, with another ~30–35% from elsewhere in China.
Bernreuter data cited by Sheffield Hallam shows the Uyghur Region's share fell to 35% in 2022 while the rest of China rose to 54%, leaving just 11% produced outside China.
The IEA reported that Xinjiang alone accounted for 40% of global polysilicon manufacturing, and China's share of every solar manufacturing stage exceeded 80%.
Chinese producers made 93.5% of the world's polysilicon output in 2024, and nine of the ten largest polysilicon makers are Chinese, according to Bernreuter Research.
About 95% of solar modules rely on one primary material, solar-grade polysilicon, so a single upstream region can taint most panels.

Sheffield Hallam found that all four Xinjiang polysilicon makers (Daqo, TBEA/Xinte, Xinjiang GCL, East Hope) reported taking part in labour transfer or placement programmes, or were supplied by firms that did.
Daqo alone supplied the world's four largest module makers at the time: JinkoSolar, Trina Solar, LONGi and JA Solar.
In Broad Daylight identified 11 companies engaged in forced labour transfers and 90 Chinese and international companies whose supply chains were affected.
From June 2022 to November 24, 2025, CBP stopped 65,707 shipment lines worth $3.91 billion for UFLPA enforcement review.
Reuters found that semiconductor devices (HTS 8541, the solar panels and cells code) made up $3.26 billion, or 82%, of the $3.94 billion in shipments stopped under the UFLPA.
More than 79% of the value of halted solar and other semiconductor shipments, about $2.5 billion, was later released to U.S. importers.
Malaysia, Vietnam and Thailand are the top countries of origin by value of shipments stopped under the UFLPA, which reflects solar cell and module manufacturing moving to Southeast Asia.
The value of stopped shipments fell to $187.7 million in 2025, down from $1.78 billion in 2024.
The August 2026 update added 43 entities to the UFLPA Entity List, the largest single expansion since the law took effect; it included TBEA, the parent of polysilicon maker Xinte.
Since June 21, 2022, the UFLPA has presumed that any goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang, or by a listed entity, are made with forced labor and are barred from entering the U.S.

timeline.event: Sheffield Hallam University publishes 'In Broad Daylight', tracing forced-labour exposure through the solar supply chain from quartz to panel.
Commerce adds Hoshine, Xinjiang Daqo, Xinjiang East Hope, Xinjiang GCL and XPCC to the BIS Entity List over forced labor.
The U.S. Department of Labor adds polysilicon from Xinjiang to its List of Goods Produced by Child Labor or Forced Labor.
CBP issues a Withhold Release Order on Hoshine's silica-based products, including goods such as polysilicon made from them.
The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act is signed into law.
The UFLPA's rebuttable presumption takes effect and the first Entity List names Hoshine, Xinjiang Daqo, Xinjiang East Hope, Xinjiang GCL and XPCC.
Sheffield Hallam publishes 'Over-Exposed' (updated November 2023), assessing ten solar manufacturers' exposure to the Uyghur Region.
DHS adds 30 entity listings and corrects East Hope's listing by removing the alias 'Xinjiang Nonferrous'.
The Solar Stewardship Initiative publishes its Supply Chain Traceability Standard, which traces silicon from quartzite mine to module, with certification starting in 2025.
Qcells furloughs about 1,000 workers at its Georgia plants after shipments of cells and polysilicon were held up under UFLPA scrutiny.
CBP's cumulative UFLPA count reaches 65,707 stopped shipment lines worth $3.91 billion.
CBP confirms its decision against detained VSUN solar modules, saying 'sufficient evidence to allow for an exception could not be confirmed'.
Reuters reports that newly broken-out CBP data shows solar makes up 82% of the value of all UFLPA-stopped shipments.
DHS announces 43 new UFLPA Entity List additions, the first update since January 2025 and the largest ever.
New listings take effect, including TBEA (Xinte's parent) and Tianchi Energy; Xinjiang GCL's listing is renamed Xinjiang Goens Energy Technology.
